utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can everyone hear me? Can the interpreters hear me? Are they refreshed and ready to go? Fine. Thank you. We are going to start the hearing. Where did we leave it at yesterday? We are going to finish the week and we are going to work until 12.30, at the latest. How many witnesses do you have left?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After this witness concludes, Mr. President, we have two witnesses remaining and we have one small matter to take up with the court at the conclusion of the testimonies of the three witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Well, you may proceed, but first we are going to have Witness BB. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So without further ado, let us have the witness come in. (Witness enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you hear me? Witness BB, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you rested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you ready to go on with your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead, then. Mr. Harmon? WITNESS BB (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness BB.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When we concluded the examination yesterday, you had started to tell the judges about your arrival at the Kaonik prison camp. That was on 15th April 1993. First of all, how long did you remain in the Kaonik prison camp from 15th April until what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the 19th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Kaonik camp, did you discover that the HVO had arrested all the Muslim men from the village of Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as we reached the camp, we found there some locals from the village of Jelinak. Not all of them, but most of them were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges what happened to you and to the others once you arrived at the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, we were searched. Money and all valuables were seized. The next day the local people from Loncari were brought in. They too were searched, and in the course of the day some drivers were brought over. They used to drive humanitarian aid convoys to Maglaj, Tesanj, Zavidovic, and there were six or seven of them who were temporarily employed in Switzerland, and they were on their way home for a holiday, and an enormous amount of money was taken from them. Something between 30 and 40,000 German marks. They had some gold watches, everything was confiscated. They also took from us our clothing, footwear, so that we were given some torn shoes. When we went to dig trenches, though it was muddy, we had to work like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness BB, were your valuables ever returned to you, the valuables that had been confiscated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was it the HVO who took the valuables from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to turn your attention to trench-digging, and if I could have the assistance of the usher, presenting to the court, the witness and counsel, Prosecutor's Exhibit 251, and your Honours and counsel, 251 is an exhibit copied from Exhibit 29(c) and it has identified on it nine locations where the witness was forced by the HVO to dig trenches. He will describe each of those locations and the events at each of those locations. Attached behind that is a legend and the legend identifies the locations and the manner in which the witness will identify them throughout his testimony. Now, Witness BB, did you make the marks on Prosecutor's Exhibit 251, the green marks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do those green marks represent the approximate locations where you were forced to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review the legend that is attached to Exhibit 251 and compare the numbers and names on the legend to the numbers that are found on the map itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And is the legend accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Witness BB, you were taken by the HVO to dig trenches at a number of locations. What I would like you to do is tell the judges in your own words about your experiences at each of those locations, and what I would like you to cover in your description and narrative answer is who took you there to dig trenches, who guarded you, when you were digging trenches, whether you were at a front-line in and around combat, how long you stayed there, what the conditions were like, what the food was like, if any, what the communications that you saw were like, and if we could start with the location which is marked on the legend number 1 which is Bare, could you tell the judges about your experiences at Bare. Wait just a minute, please. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, Mr. Harmon. Please carry on. This is a light way of putting questions. Try and answer accurately all the questions raised by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we reached the camp on the second or third day we were taken to the location known as Bare. A man called Sumar, I do not know his real name, they boarded us into a big truck. The make was Ravna. And they drove us to the school, in front of the school at Bare. There they told us they would give us some food, and we were given a loaf of bread and 400 grams of salami to be shared for four or five people. Something like that. I do not remember exactly. And then we were taken in the direction of the village of Rovna or rather Kovacevac which was already burned down and under Croatian control. When we reached our destination, two Croatian soldiers who were taking us there took shelter and suddenly shooting started so we too ran for shelter but they prohibited us from doing that. They said, "do not run, your people will not kill you". That was when Ramo Zlatagic and Salih Sunulpasic were wounded. Ramo in the neck and Salih in the head. The shooting lasted about 10-15 minutes, then it stopped. They took us on further. However, when we got to the exact place from where the fire had come, there was a large group of HVO soldiers there, so my conclusion was that it was they who had fired at us because it was not possible that they had fired at us from where the trenches were being dug. So, we were kept there for a short while, what was -- the trenches that needed to be dug we dug, and then we were transferred to another location also in Bare, but at the other end, on the other side of the village of Rovna. There too we were digging two dug-outs and some trenches. During the digging of a dug-out that I was working on, I noticed a soldier with an HV sign, and when I asked him to give me some water to drink, as I got up, he hit me with his rifle butt on the back and told me to go on digging so I acted as I was told, though it was very hard. But I had no choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions quickly to clarify your experiences at Bare. Did you go to the Bare location on one occasion or more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly. Maybe once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you say you went, were you accompanied by other Muslims, and how many were there that went with you to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I went, with me were only the inhabitants of the village of Jelinak and only a few from Loncari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately how many Muslims were there that went with you to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How old were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 18 and 50 or 60. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Witness BB, they were all Muslims, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now I would like to turn your attention, Witness BB, to the second location marked on the map, and it is identified and the legend is Kula. Could you please tell the judges your experiences trench-digging at Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were being taken to Kula, I do not know exactly how many times we were taken there, but we went there many times to dig trenches. This was the second location we were taken to, that is Kula, and there too there was a lot of digging to do. Our hands were already bleeding from the blisters because we had no protective gloves. The conditions were awful, the food was terribly poor. We would just get a slice of bread, a very thin slice of bread, and just some sort of a soup, but there was nothing in it, really. For me that could not be called soup and in spite of such poor food we had to dig and endure all kinds of insults. The first time we went there, we stayed for a day and a night. The second time, already, we stayed longer. Four to five days we stayed there and we had to dig day and night with very, very small breaks to rest, but that could hardly be called a rest. I hardly had time to look around me before it was time to continue digging again. As I said, we were taken there many times, though in between we were also taken to other locations, but I remember Kula as the place I went to most often.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, how many people, how many forced labourers went with you to the Kula lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 30 men, sometimes up to 40, though again, sometimes we would meet the local people from Busovaca there, because when I was brought to the location where I was to dig I found three men from Busovaca there and also people from the village of Skradno. They were also brought there to dig, and were also given such very poor rations, though from -- some people from Skradno were able to take some food with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were the people who were forced to dig trenches at Kula, were they Muslims and were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, while you were at the Kula location, was that in and around exposed confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was actually on the front-line, because the point was to provide trenches for the HVO soldiers for them to dig in so as to be protected from the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the civilian trench-diggers were exposed to fire going in either direction. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to tell the judges, if you could, about the time that UNPROFOR came to the Kula region and what happened to you and the other trench diggers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not exactly know which route we took to go to Kula, but on that occasion we had started digging and the firing broke out suddenly from all sides. At that moment I was lost, so to speak, but I could notice that there were Croatian soldiers who were wounded. We heard the sound of a motor, and when I turned around to the right, away from us, I saw UNPROFOR transporters heading towards the location at Kula. The Croatian soldiers then hid us in a small pine wood, and there we were exposed to even heavier fire. As far as I was able to notice everyone was shooting. Both the Muslims and the Croats, at us, because, of course, the Muslims were firing at the Croatian lines and we were on those lines. Then one of the HVO soldiers told us that the commander at the time, Sefer Halilovic would be coming to inspect the lines, although I did not know him in person, I did not personally see him, but I saw the UNPROFOR transporters and other vehicles. The shooting stopped abruptly. When the UNPROFOR left we stayed on to dig. We were brought back where we had been before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, you were essentially hidden from view from UNPROFOR while they were at the location of Kula. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Could you now turn to the third location that is marked on the legend, which is Podjele? Could you tell the judges your experience as a trench digger at Podjele? Who took you there, who guarded you, whether it was a combat area, how many people were taken there...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regarding the actual location of Podjele, a man were Kotor Varos came to pick us up who was living in the village of Podjele. He selected about 30 of us and he took us to the village of Podjele and in the village itself he lined us up, and he ordered us to point -- stretch out our hands, to roll up our sleeves with our palms up. He probably wanted to see whether we still had any valuables left, a ring or a watch or something. After that he ordered us to take out everything we had in our pockets, though we had nothing in our pockets. My trousers did not have any pockets in, so this man, known as Zare, told me to turn out my pockets. I said I did not have any pockets in my trousers, so he repeated the order. He said, "do it or I will kill you". So there was nothing I could do, because he was pointing his gun at me. I heard the shot. At that moment I did not really know what had happened. I was so frightened. I did not know whether I was dead. I know that I fell down. After a couple of minutes, when I heard voices again, I realised I was still alive. All I know is that I could not see anything, because when he fired the shot, the bullet hit the ground between my feet, and there were pebbles on the path, and these pebbles scattered and I think it was also probably fragmentation of the bullet, and I had injuries on my hands and there were small pebbles or maybe even shrapnel over my body and hands, and I know I took out a piece from my lower lip. What it was, I do not know. Then he ordered us to go to a location where we had to dig trenches. This is a location facing the village of Merdani and he said, he told these people that if I moved they should kill me. So one of our men tried to lead me on. I do not know who it was. I just heard him say, "let him go. He can walk alone", so I heard them moving. I managed to hold on to the shoulder of my brother whose voice I recognised. He was in front of me, and I followed him. We were taken from the village to do the digging. He was a house painter, I do not remember his name exactly, and his brother's name was Hrvoje. He used to work with me. They brought us to the spot where we were expected to dig, and then Hrvoje and his brother protected me for a while, because I could not see anything because of the blood, and we did not have any water to wash my wounds. Then I sat there for about fifteen or twenty minutes with my hands -- I managed to wipe away the blood, and then I too joined in the digging. They said, "Well, you do not have to dig yet", but I remembered what Zare had said, because if he were to see that I was sitting there, he would kill me, because I saw that he also had a sniper so he could see me from the village. Again, there were about 30 men there. I do not know the exact number. We did not have a chance to count.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were the 30 men that were taken to dig with you, were they all Muslims and were they all civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was Zare a member of the HVO, and how do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He had the insignia of the HVO on his sleeve. As far as I know, they were from Kotor Varos and they were refugees in the village of Podjele, which used to be inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were the people who guarded you while you and your colleagues were digging trenches, were they in the HVO as well? Were they HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were the people who guarded you while you were digging at Podjele HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you receive any food while you were digging at Podjele on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion, we were given no food at all. I know this man who was a painter. I do not know his name. He went and he told us that he had stolen some dates, and being so hungry, we could not eat them because it is so sweet. It would only make us sick. At least I did not eat any. Some did, and there was no other food. Later on they gave us just some biscuits packed in a tin of about 5 kilos in weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say, "later on", are you referring to another occasion when you and others went to dig trenches at Podjele?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was another occasion when we went to Podjele again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many times did you go to Podjele to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went three or four times, though once we went as far as the actual road to Podjele, not far from Kaonik where the railway bridge used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness BB, on all of the occasions when you went to dig trenches at Podjele, were you in the presence or accompanied by a large number of Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And on each occasion when you went to Podjele were you taken there by the HVO and were you guarded there by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you went to Podjele, your group of 30 or so Muslims went to Podjele. When you arrived there did you find other Muslims who were digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but once a shift came from the barracks, people who were also imprisoned there, some 30 of them, they came to replace us, but we stayed in the barracks itself three or four hours and then we were brought back to Podjele again. We did not really have replacements, because the people who came to replace us were still there and we had to continue working on another set of trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn now, Witness BB, to location number 4, Carica? Could you tell the judges about your experiences at Carica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know regarding Carica we went to two locations near Carica. I do not know the exact names of the places. At Carica itself they told us to dig some kind of star-shaped trenches. I had never heard of such trenches, and I did not manage to dig one. Then later they said that we should just dig some ordinary trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately how many people went with you to Carica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, the number was more or less the same. Wherever I went, whether other groups went to other locations, I do not know, but I know that with me there were always about 30 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were they always Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Because only the Muslims were detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was the area of Carica an area that was exposed to combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really. They were more like provocations there. That was when Fuad, Fikret, known as Hodza, was wounded. He comes from Tesanj. I do not know his exact name, but I know he was called Hodza. They were also brought to the barracks. They were not given any treatment, they were just left in the cell, wounded, they were just dressed with bandages, no disinfectant was used or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The other three wounded trench diggers were Muslims again. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness BB, could you turn to the fifth location, marked Strane. Could you tell the judges your experiences at Strane, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Going to the location at Strane, again, up to 30 people were taken there, and when we arrived a Muslim was killed who was detained with us. I do not know his name, but I know he came from Tesen. He is a businessman, one could call him that, because he owned two large Mercedes vehicles and there was a wife and four children left when he died. He had quite a bit of land, and his neighbour was detained with us, and with the permission of the Red Cross he transported his dead body, this neighbour of his, to Tesen. At the time there were two dug-outs that we were digging and trenches facing Merdani and the village of Putis. I know that I went there once. I was not taken more often to the village of Strane and as I said, again, they were about 30 people taken there, though if we wanted to mention the exact figure, one of them got killed, so 29 of us returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were at Strane did you see any soldiers with walkie-talkies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw one, but I do not know whether he was a commander, possibly, because as far as I know, ordinary privates could not have that equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you also see walkie-talkies at Bare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This man, nicknamed Sumar, had a walkie-talkie on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to turn to location number 6, which is marked on the map. In the legend it is marked at Kuber. Could you again tell the judges your experiences at Kuber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The actual location was one we were also taken to five or six times, I do not know exactly, but only during the night, and we were brought back before dawn, because there were very fierce combat operations during there at the daytime. The HVO lost some positions so that if we spent one night digging, the next night we would have to move back 100 metres and dig more trenches. We were extremely exhausted, but we had to go on digging, and because they were really angry and fierce. They treated us, I do not know how to describe it, but inhumanely, certainly. They would curse us, insult us. I did not see them hitting anyone, but they did not hit me on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Next could you turn to your experiences at Loncari? Item number 7 on Prosecutor's Exhibit 251.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were taken to the Loncari location, that was above the village of Loncari, there was a chapel there, a Serb chapel, and I think that that was one of their strongest fortifications. There was one dug-out next to another, and they were all connected by these trenches. We were taken there once or twice. I do not recall. Also, all the ones who were taken there were Muslims, about 30 of us. I do not know who the commander was, because many of them ordered us, that so I do not know who exactly was the commander there. Later on I heard that he was called Sisko. I do not know this person. I just heard this from someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Witness BB, how did you get to Loncari? Were you transported in vehicles or did you walk, you and your fellow trench-diggers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were brought to the village of Loncari in a large vehicle, and at Strane we were just brought to below Strane and then we had to walk up, and -- over to Loncari we were actually driven to the actual location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So when you went to dig trenches at the village of Strane, did you leave Kaonik camp on foot and walk to your trench-digging locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to the end of the main road, and from there we went on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Could you tell the judges next about location number 8, Kaonik? First of all, tell the judges how you got there, to that trench digging, or that labour location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken there and we just needed to work on the bridge, or to pour concrete there. There were six of us there. Because there used to be a railroad track passing through there, while there was still steam engine-propelled trains there, so we were taken there to put concrete... and I could not see UNPROFOR passing through on that road. If they did, they would hide us. So if the UNPROFOR would come in our -- would pass us, we would have to lie down in the vehicle, so that the body of the vehicle would hide us. As I said, we were just fixing the bridge and at one point we just dug some dug-outs next to the bridge. I think they just wanted it there for us, security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness BB, how did you get from Kaonik camp to this work location? Did you walk from the camp to the work location? Did you walk along the main road to the work location or were you transported there by vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken there in a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this work location is right next to the main road that goes to Busovaca. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, lastly, I would like you to describe to the judges what you were asked to do at Ravan, which is location number 9. Who took you there, what were you forced to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the last location. There were six or seven of us who were taken there. We dug at a place called Ravan, and these were -- we dug graves, apparently three of them, because apparently three of their soldiers were killed. We did not stay there long, after about three hours we were taken back to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness BB, you mentioned that when you were at Kuber on one occasion when an UNPROFOR came you were concealed, and I think you were telling the judges that when you were transported in HVO vehicles to various trench-digging locations, if an UNPROFOR vehicle passed by you and the other trench diggers were asked to duck down so that the UNPROFOR personnel would not see you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, this has been said again and again. I fail to understand. Not only do we come back to previous occasions but you ask the witness to say again what he said perfectly. He told you that every time, so we are not going to come back in detail to every location because there are nine of them. Witness BB said that whenever there was an UNPROFOR convoy driving by they were told to hide. The judges have understood that. Please, do not carry on that way. After all, we are able to understand, Judge Shahabuddeen and myself. We know what the witness said, so whenever, on each of the nine locations, maybe not all of them, but we understand that the UNPROFOR convoys did not go through the nine locations, but we are not going to move ahead in this way because this has been said by the witness. You have, according to your summary, one last item to tackle. This is the meeting with Kordic, so please, Witness BB, can you speak about this meeting with Kordic, otherwise we are going to take the lead. We cannot go on this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I be permitted to finish one part of my examination which deals with efforts by the HVO to conceal civilian forced labour, as he has described --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, we are sufficiently informed on the camps, so please move on to the fourth item of your summary, because I remind you that you announced four items that you were going to deal with with this witness and the witness perfectly dealt with the first three items. Now, if you fear that in the cross-examination questions are raised, well, you have the time thereafter to ask further questions, so I am asking you to deal with the fourth item, the meeting in Kaonik with Dario Kordic so please, Witness BB, please tell us about that meeting. As far as the rest are concerned, we are sufficiently informed. So please, Witness BB, speak about Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. When I was in the camp we were taken out just to get some air, and then I saw that there was a vehicle, I do not know the make of it, and I saw Dario Kordic there, because I knew him. He used to work with me before the war. When he arrived we were taken back immediately, so that I do not know where he went, and why he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Witness BB, as a result of your experiences in the Kaonik camp and as a result of being forced to dig trenches and being poorly fed, how much weight did you lose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not have scales to weigh ourselves, so I would say for sure up to 15 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would now move to introduce Prosecutor's Exhibit 251, the map and the legend into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is there any objections from the Defence? And which is the number for this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 251. That is right. Thank you. Have you finished Mr. Harmon? Thank you very much. Now, turning to Mr. Nobilo, are you going to take the cross-examination? So Witness BB, you are now going to hear the questions asked by the Defence. General Blaskic has two lawyers defending him, and the Prosecutor will be entitled to ask further questions, if there are any items that are raised during cross-examination so please go ahead, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Witness BB, you described how you came to Kaonik, and that the HVO members were taken away, and especially the people who had come from Switzerland on holiday. Do you know whether this money and gold was just deposited there and was then given back to them, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anything that was taken away from prisoners was put on a table, and one soldier collected it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know whether this was taken, given back or do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my communications I do not know that anything was given back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was taken away from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a watch. That is all I had on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned that a soldier hit you with a rifle butt. Were you otherwise beaten while you were digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I only was hit at the Bare location.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Other than that there was nothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing, except in the camp there were beatings and some acts of provocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So, in your statement on the 26th January 1993 which you gave to the police in Zenica, and which you accept as your own, you said, "in my work details there was no physical mistreatment by the members of the HVO"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you give such a statement to the security forces in Zenica, though?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, I did give a statement but not such a statement, but I know exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would -- may I ask the usher to show the statement which we received from the Prosecution, and the witness had given the statement and signed it. Could the witness please confirm that this is his signature? It is the last page. (Handed). Please, if you could just look if this is your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like to tender it in evidence, and later we will provide additional copies, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There could be a mistake in the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned the locations where you dug. Could you tell me, on average, how far were the BH Army positioned in relation to the places where you dug?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not tell you in metres exactly, but approximately up to 500 metres, sometimes 1 kilometre even. It depended on the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But you would agree with the conclusion that on average the BH Army positions were between 500 metres and 1 kilometre. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. (10.15 am)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At Kuber, you said that the HVO were losing their positions and so you had to dig new trenches again. Could you tell us when this was? Was this in April or May? Could you tell us at least a month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not say because we were in fear, so I was not really -- I could not remember the dates. Even my name, sometimes, was hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you dug trenches, how far above the village were you in Loncari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as Loncari is concerned, maybe up to 100, 200 metres from the last house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So, the front-line was right next to the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was right next to it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you dug at Strane, how far was the line from the last house at Strane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the very last house next to the village of Putis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And one last question, did you ever personally see General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see General Blaskic around there at all. I only saw him on television when we were in a village of Jelinak, and we were watching the Vitez TV and I do not know, it could have been HTV. I know that there was a TV in Busovaca so I personally saw the gentleman there on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, this concludes our examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Nobilo. Any further questions, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No questions. Judge Shahabuddeen? I do not have any either. So Witness BB, thank you very much for coming to testify in front of this court, because this reminded you of very painful events. Please do not move right now. We are going to adjourn. We are going to break for some twenty minutes, that is until twenty to eleven, and you can then leave the courtroom being protected. (10.20 am) (Short adjournment) (10.45 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, first, in respect of the Defence exhibit that was introduced, a statement of Witness BB, I would ask that that be placed under seal since it has identifying information of the witness. Second of all, Mr. President, I would move to introduce a copy of Witness BB's statement he gave to the OTP in 1997 as an exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What are you asking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: A copy of Witness BB's statement that he provided to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we object because in this statement there are some other facts which were -- to which the witness did not testify today, and we had no opportunity to cross-examine him on this, so in this way, certain facts would enter into evidence without our ever testing their veracity, and without our asking a certain number of questions that would test these facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: -- can we hold this in abeyance? Otherwise it may reveal the Defence's strategy and this is no urgent matter. By the end of the proceedings, I mean, this could be recorded by the Registry, especially if there are other elements. What do you think, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I am prepared to submit this without it being accepted, marked for identification only, and we can come back and debate this at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo? It is marked and identified. There is a problem of identification here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We have no problem with it being marked for identification, but maybe I was a bit -- the interpretation came a bit late so maybe I missed the whole thing, so I do not know what the purpose of this being introduced would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to ask a question. This was a statement provided to the Office of the Prosecutor, was it, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Nobilo, the Prosecution knows what there is in that statement. I am coming back to your initial objection. First I was convinced and now I am having some doubts. The Prosecution knows what there is in that statement and you are now telling me, "I am objecting because I have used only certain elements and I am going to use other elements later on"? Am I wrong? Maybe I got it wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Maybe there was a misunderstanding here. What I had said was that in this statement there are certain parts, there are facts to which the witness did not testify here, and so we were unable to examine the witness on those issues, which is why we object to introducing this statement into evidence, because we have not been given an opportunity to cross-examine the witness on -- and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I add, Mr. President, by contrast, we offered an exhibit, a 1993 statement of the witness taken literally within days of some of these events, as impeachment because the written signed statement of the witness contradicted his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which statements are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This is the Defence exhibit. There are two statements, Mr. President; defence exhibit, I believe it is D86 which we offered and to which there was no objection. I believe that is in evidence. That is the statement which the witness signed, stating that there was no mistreatment of prisoners in one or more contexts. This statement, I believe, we only have in BSC, Mr. President. It was provided, I think, recently to us. So that is the reason we offered that statement. There was no objection. Now, after the witness has gone, the Prosecutor is coming in with a different statement to which, as Mr. Nobilo points out, we have not examined and cross-examined the witness as to all the contents of this other statement, let alone why is the other statement relevant. The witness was just here. They could have elicited any facts in that 1997 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the statement you are talking about, which is that? Is that the one I have now in my hand?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is another declaration, Mr. President. It is a statement that he gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on 29th July 1997. Now, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But we did not discuss that, did we?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, we did not introduce it. What was introduced by the Defence was a statement in Bosnian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So you did not even ask your own witness as to that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I have interrogated him on a variety --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But that statement should have been given to the Defence, pursuant to Rule 66. It should have been for a long time. You have that statement, Mr. Nobilo. I am not talking about the one you have there, I am talking about another statement. Please, enlighten me on this, because the poor civil lawyer that I am, does not understand. This is a situation which is inconceivable. The judges are going to assess the relevance of this testimony only on the basis of what the witness said, and not on the basis of his statement, but this is a major stake for you, so this statement has been communicated to you. You have it, have you not? So let us forget this one because that one has been exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We did receive, yes, we did receive the statement, but the witness was not examined either in the examination-in-chief, nor in cross-examination on those facts, so we had the witness here, and this testimony could have been introduced through the examination-in-chief and then could have been subjected to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to discuss with my colleague for a minute. (Pause). The court turns down the tendering which is challenged by the Defence. As has been explained by the Defence, the witness is gone, and you said, Prosecutor, that you had based your questions on that statement. Let me make a general statement. You know that these proceedings are difficult, not only because they are lengthy, because of the large number of questions that are asked and often repetitive, and the difficulty lies also in the number and in the diversity of statements taken from witnesses, so we come up with problems such as this one. There is an attempt, an impeachment by the Defence on the basis of three or four statements. This is no easy matter so we are not admitting this exhibit for the moment, and let us move on to the next item, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I make some comments, Mr. President, just some observations and then I will be happy to move on, or may I reserve those for a later time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is not customary to have comments following a decision issued by the judges. The judges have conferred. They have made a decision, and the court is amply informed as to the testimony by Witness BB, and you are very lucky, Mr. Harmon, I am saying this today, and also I will say this to the Defence. You are very lucky, because facing the sufferings endured by the witnesses, given the way they are disturbed, given the time that is asked for them to come here, we should wonder as to the relevance of this. You are very lucky that I, unlike other judges in the Tribunal, do not say, "Well, this is over, Witness, you can leave the courtroom". I believe that we need procedures. We have been able to manage this very well. Yesterday and the day before yesterday, but we have to be simple, so the matter is settled. The decision has been issued, and we have already lost a quarter of an hour in this. On to the next item.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. The next witness is a protected witness who has asked for face and pseudonym protection. I can give you a summary very quickly, Mr. President. The witness is a Bosnian Muslim who resided in the Kiseljak municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So how is he going to be called?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Witness CC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness CC resided in the village of Polje Visnjica, which is a village different to the Witness AA resided in. It is the village lower than Witness AA's village and closer to the main road. Her testimony will cover four areas. The first is the attack on the village of Polje Visnjica, which commenced on the 18th April 1993. She will describe the results of that attack. Second of all, she will describe the circumstances of the attempted forcible exchange of her daughter by the HVO, and her daughter's wounding, which occurred on the 30th June 1993. Thirdly, she will testify about her expulsion by the HVO from her house, and lastly she will testify about the expulsion of the Muslims who remain in the village of Polje Visnjica thereafter. Her testimony relates to count 1, persecution, which includes paragraph 6.1, 6.3, 6.4 through paragraph 7. Counts 2-4, unlawful attacks on civilians and civilian objects, paragraph 8. Counts 11 through 13, destruction and plunder of property, paragraph 10. Counts 15 and 16, inhumane treatment of detainees and hostages, paragraphs 13 through 15. Because this witness is a protected witness, Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, I have instructed her during the course of her deposition not to identify by name her relatives, that she will be describing events that occurred to them, and she is, however, as I mentioned yesterday, prepared to do so in a private session if that is required. So with that, Mr. President, I would ask that she be brought in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Witness CC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are here welcome, and we are going to call you Witness CC, because the court has ordered some protective measures. First, you are going to identify --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are first going to identify your name without pronouncing it, on that piece of paper. Please read your name but do not pronounce it. Fine. And now you are going to swear the oath on the basis of the paper handed in by the Registrar. WITNESS CC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You are going to be asked some questions by the Prosecutor and then you will be free to relate the events as regards the three or four items interesting for the judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness CC.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a citizen of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And are you a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In April of 1993 did you live in the Kiseljak municipality in the village of Polje Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Prior to the attack on your village, how long had you lived in that particular village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got married in 1968 and I lived there until 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was the village of Polje Visnjica a mixed Muslim and Croat village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have asked you to come to this court to testify about four particular areas and I would like to start with the first area, which is having you describe to the judges the attack on your village that occurred on April 18th, and if you would proceed telling the judges about that attack and then we will move to the next area. Please, tell the judges, in a narrative form, about the events that occurred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 18th April 1993 some people were listening to the radio, Radio Kiseljak, and the population was told not to be disturbed because the UNPROFOR would be doing some exercises in Kiseljak. I got up at 6 o'clock on the 18th. I was awoken by strong detonations. I asked my husband whether he knew what was happening. He said he did not. A woman came to see me. She too did not know what was happening. Afterwards two men came by. I asked them what was happening. They were in civilian clothes. They were not armed, and they told us to go to a shelter. We went to a house where there was one storey and we were in the basement in a shelter and we spent two days there. On the third day we were told that we had to surrender, that we should go towards the silo to the checkpoint. One of our men, one of our Muslims carried a white flag on a pole. We followed him to -- in a row, two by two. We reached the barricades. They followed us with their weapons. They cursed our balija mothers and the dzana hidrija, the alesa state. We reached the checkpoint, a big truck with a canvas cover came. It took off our men to the barracks. We stayed behind. Women, children, and some elderly people. They left my husband with me because I asked them to leave him. We spent two nights there in five different houses where we were put up. Kasim Handzic, Serif Cilas, Meho Cilas, Ibro Cilas, all these houses were full of us Muslims who were brought there to the checkpoint. We spent two nights there. We asked whether we could go back to our homes, and while we were at the silo we saw thick smoke, and I saw Rasid Bulic's house and stable on fire. I did not see anything else except the smoke. After that, we asked to go back to our own village and they let us go. We returned to the village. When we got there, our houses had been looted, the doors had been broken, everything had been turned upside down in the houses. Rasid Bulic's house and stable and a cow had been burned. In Omer Drinjak's house the stable and cow, Rasid Drinjak's stable and two cows. Sljivar's stable and a cow. Alija Dzina, a stable and a cow. Said Ahmedic's house, shed and cow, but the cow did not quite burn. She survived. Nasid Handzic's house and stable were burned. Enver Handzic's house. Ismet Handzic's house and stable. Dzemil Karahmet's house and stable. Hasim Sljivar's house and stable. Then further on, near my sister's stable had been burned, and a cow. In one of my relatives' stable and cow, then further on, the Begovic village, everything was torched. Ibro's house and stable, Enver's stable and house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we understand that all the stables were torched. Please carry on. Carry on to the next events, although these were bad enough, but please carry on. So everything was burned down. No need to enumerate all the people whose shed or stables and cows were burned. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. So we continued living there in the village. There were various provocations. They would come to take our men to dig trenches. They forced my husband, my brother-in-law who managed to get away one night through the woods with his brother. Then there were provocations around my daughter. They were -- they wanted her to get out. Then they wanted to force her to go to Bilalevac to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness CC, let me stop you right there, because we are going to move into another topic I am going to asking you about in a few minutes. Let me clarify some points on your testimony about the attack. When you got to the area, the silos, can you describe the uniforms that you saw being worn by the men who were guarding you and the other civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The men were wearing camouflage HVO uniforms. They had the insignia and they had rifles. I saw two in black uniforms, and on their cap they had the letter, "U". I only saw two of them like that. There were many soldiers there. All were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you gave an incomplete list of the number of people's properties that you saw that were burned. Two questions. One, were they all Muslims, the houses that you described and the ones that you did not testify about, by identifying the owners of those houses? Were they all Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. All were Muslim houses. All of them were torched. There was not a single Croatian house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when you left your house, surrendered and went to the silos, were the houses that you have identified, not burned? Were they intact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we went to the silos, Rasid Drinjak's house and the others were all intact. Only Ismet Handzic's stable and Dzemil Karahmet's stable were burned. The rest was intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So two days later when you returned, then those houses that you identified and all the other Muslim houses had been burned down. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, adjacent to the Muslim houses that you have identified that had been burned down were there Croat houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (readcted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were any Croat houses that you could see burned or robbed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, while you -- did you remain in the village, after you returned to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did your husband remain with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While he remained with you was he ever taken by the HVO to go dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband went perhaps only three times to dig trenches, while we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the HVO come and collect other people who lived in Polje Visnjica and take them to dig trenches beside your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Hasan Karahmet was killed digging trenches. Haris Begovic was wounded digging trenches. Salko Fezic was seriously wounded also digging trenches. That is as much as I know, personally. These were all people were my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Those are all Muslim people. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn to the second event, and that is the attempted forcible transfer of your daughter by the HVO and her wounding that took place on the 30th June 1993. Would you please tell the judges about that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After my son-in-law fled, my daughter stayed at home, and they tried to chase her out, and they gave her four days' time to stay at home, and then Pasko came to bring his father from Bilalac. The first day my daughter refused, then Pasko came again, the next day, to take her. She went to talk to Nikica Pravdic, called Braco, and he told her that she had to go to the Fojnica barricade, and he went with her as well as Ando Palalija and this Pasko who had come there. He went with them. There they wrote down something on a piece of paper, and said that she should contact Bilalovac for an exchange. My daughter came home. She told me about it. Then Marinko Bodula came. What his intentions were, I do not know Marinko Bodula also asked that my daughter should bring the old man from Brestovsko. He came in a blue car. He picked his -- he got his pistol. There was an extremist with him and I must call him an extremist because he fired. He shot at my daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness CC, before you continue, were these people who came to collect your daughter, were they HVO soldiers, and how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soldiers. HVO soldiers, camouflage uniform. This one had a rifle, and when I told him that she could not be replaced for the whole of Bilalovac, he took his rifle and shot at her roof, and the tiles started falling on us. Her older daughter --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, just to interrupt you very quickly, did she have two small children, that is my first question, and my second question is, did she want to participate in this exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She had a daughter of four and a half, and a younger one of two and a half, and she did not want to go for such an exchange, because she had small children. The little one was already in bed with a bottle. He cursed and swore at her God and threatened that she had to go. I begged him, "please do not take her. My son got killed last year. I have no more children, only her". He cursed again and said that she had to go or he would slaughter all of us, and then she said, "Well, all right mummy, I will go and I will come back", and then I said, "but I am coming with you". He said, "you can go, but she has to go", and as we were getting into the car my granddaughter was crying saying, "mummy, I want to come with you". My daughter said, "come here, dear. Sit in your mother's lap". We got in and he continued threatening, and this extremist was saying, "we will kill all of you balijas if they beat him over there". I just cried all the time. When we reached a hill, no exchange had been arranged. This was done by force because he did not give her a white flag or anything. There was not any prior notification. He simply let her go between the lines. I asked to go with her, but they would not let me. Marinko Tadic spoke to Marinko Bodula and told him that I should go because I was wearing the Muslim costume. He said, "no". He refused. Then my daughter went off. I stayed there for a while. I heard some shots. There were two shots fired, and a third time there was a burst of fire. I cried and shouted, "my daughter will get killed! I have no more children!", and he said to me that their people would not shoot, that our people would shoot. I said I did not care who was shooting, all I cared about was my child. So, a little later, Marinko Tadic came, who accompanied my daughter up to a point. Then he came back and said something to Marinko Bodula, I watched the glances they exchanged. I saw that something was happening. I said to him, "I am sure my daughter has been killed". He cursed my country, he just said, "she has only been slightly wounded. You see what your people are doing?", and I said to him, "may God punish you. What are you doing to my daughter?". They brought my daughter on a stretcher. She was covered in blood. My granddaughter was watching and crying. I took her away so that she should not watch this, and one of the HVO soldiers picked her up in his arms, so she no longer approached her mother. One of them was giving me a cigarette, and I refused. I said, "God will reward you for what you are doing", and then they took her to a hospital. They first went to Kiseljak, the barracks there. They gave her some kind of treatment, I suppose. I asked them whether I could see her once to kiss her. They let me do it, and she opened her eyes and I saw that she was still alive for a moment. Then they took her to Fojnica, and I did not see her again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness CC, let me ask you some questions surrounding that particular event. The location where your daughter was taken and from, where she was directed to walk across the front lines, were there soldiers at that location? What kind of soldiers were they and how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got there in front of a house there were several soldiers there. Two of them, maybe, were in civilian clothes. The rest were in uniforms. I do not know them. I could not really recognise them. I was not in my right mind. You can imagine how you feel. Imagine if it was your child. You cannot concentrate. Your brain does not work. So I do not know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were they HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I do not know how many there were. Yes, they were HVO soldiers because we were in their territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And then when you referred to the barracks, you are referring to the Kiseljak army barracks where she was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As a result of the wound is your daughter disabled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My daughter is 80 per cent disabled. She had a third of her liver cut off, a third of her lungs, a third of her stomach. She was wounded in the hand, and in the stomach with the cluster bullet. Her whole stomach is covered in wounds. She has no accommodation. (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now let me turn to the third event in your testimony and that is the expulsion of you from your house in Polje Visnjica which occurred on or about 28th August 1993. Could you please tell the judges how you were expelled from your house by the HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One day, after my daughter had left, when she went to the hospital she was captured in Bokovice then she came back. I do not know whether it was after a month. The UNPROFOR took her to her children. We stayed on to live there. Two days later in the evening, some men with stockings over their heads -- I was praying at that moment, I was bending down. They came. One of them took me by the neck and told me to lie down. My husband was sitting to the right. The door of the kitchen was open. I was praying in the corridor. My husband saw what was happening, so when he released me I saw the stockings over their heads and eyes. I screamed. I lost my voice. My husband, another one, took me by the neck. He pointed his pistol at my forehead. He demanded money. I said we did not have any. My husband said, "are you going to kill my wife as well? Please do not kill her", and then this other one said, "lie down", and he pointed his gun at him and so he lay down. I saw that. And then this other one released me. I passed through the kitchen onto the balcony, so I thought if he started shooting I would jump and then I cried out -- Nikica Pravdic, known as Braco, who was responsible for our village, Visnjica, and I called out, "Braco, help, these stockinged people have come demanding money and we have not got any. Come quickly". So I looked, my husband got up. I just asked him with a nod where they were. I did not utter a word, and he nodded to indicate that they had left. I went into the yard, I was crying and screaming, or trying to, because I had no voice. Afterwards, a man called Anto, a refugee from Podlugovi came and he asked me what had happened. He asked me and I told him. Then he stayed a while with us and then he left. After that, they came to my house, the police. They asked my husband, "how many of you are there in this house?". He said, "just me and my wife"; "very well", and they left. The next day, again the police came, HVO police. They gave us 15 minutes to take with us some food and to abandon the house. So we said, "okay". I cried. I was standing there with another woman. Then Slavot Miletic came up to me and his wife, and his brother's wife. He was carrying a rifle, pointed at us, but he said, "do not be afraid. They will not kill you. I have got a document to move into your house", and I said, "I am not afraid. You can kill me anyway because I have lost my son. I do not need to live". So he took this paper and said, "if you are going to cry then my tears will reach me but I will not move in, someone else will anyway", so I said, "never mind, I am not crying because of that. Move in". I just asked whether I could use the summer kitchen, and he said, "of course". So my husband and I moved into the summer kitchen. We spent seven days there, maybe eight. And then orders came that all of us Muslims had to go to the village of Rotilj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me stop you there Witness CC, and clarify some points in respect of your expulsion from your house. You said that first of all some policemen came and said you had fifteen minutes to move out of your house; were these HVO military policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. HVO, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said that an individual who you have identified had a piece of paper. Did you take a look at that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said that. No, no, I did not look at it. I was not interested. I told him he could move in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did he represent that that piece of paper was a piece of paper from some authoritative body that permitted him to move into your house and kick you out of your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose. It was given to him. It must have been important for him. I do not know. He was holding it and then he sort of threw it on the table when he saw me crying, but I said, "never mind, you move in". I just asked whether I could use the summer kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what happened to the few remaining Muslims who still continued to reside in your village? Tell the judges what happened in respect of their houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of us left on the 6th September to the village of Rotilj under pressure. They said we had to leave that village because they did not want to have any Muslims in that village of Visnjica. HVO soldiers came to every house and stuck on a label with the name of the person who was moving in, and we just had to move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness CC, wait just a minute, please. (Pause). (11.30)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For technical reasons, as was explained by the Registrar, which I am not very aware of, but there are technical reasons, I think it should be better to have private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection from the Defence? The Registrar could explain this very quickly. I do not want the decisions made by the judges not to be accounted for.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. We can ensure that the witness is safe if there is a name or a location that could be identified, but technically, we can no longer redact, so to ensure all safety, we are asking for a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is it no longer possible today?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So okay, we will have the private session. (In Private Session)
